results.question: On BGL, what usually shows up on a node shortly before a 'kernel panic'?
results.answer:
On BGL, a "kernel panic" usually has nothing logged on the same node just before it.

- **How often it occurs:** "kernel panic" (pattern 576) has 18 lines on 18 different nodes, between 2005-08-15 and 2005-11-11. All are FATAL, from KERNEL, and owned by node-platform. The nodes I checked are I/O-node locations, ending in `-I:J18-U01` or `-I:J18-U11`.
- **Most panics have no precursor:** I looked back 10 minutes and 60 minutes on the same node, and both gave identical results. For 13 of the 18 panics, no other pattern was logged on that node in that window. I opened two cases (2005-08-15 16:31:53 on R04-M0-N8-I:J18-U01 and 2005-08-19 13:56:00 on R43-M0-NC-I:J18-U01). Neither node logged anything in the 15 minutes before the panic.
- **The only recurring precursor:** 4 of 18 panics (22%) were preceded by "L<N> correctable errors exceeds threshold (iar <HEX> lr <HEX>)" (pattern 178, INFO). It came about 0.4 s before the panic (median). The same check shifted one day earlier found it 0% of the time, so the lift is 4.0. That is only 4 occurrences, so it is a weak signal, not a reliable warning.
- **A one-off:** 1 of 18 panics (6%) was preceded, about 20.7 s earlier, by a FATAL ciod error: "Error loading … invalid or missing program image, Permission denied" (pattern 812). With a single case, I wouldn't call that a pattern.

Related KERNEL messages exist, such as "rts panic! - stopping execution" and "rts: kernel terminated for reason <N>". I did not check whether they come before "kernel panic". Association in time is not proof of cause.

results.question: Is reliability on BGL improving between September and November 2005 (2005-09-01 to 2005-11-29)?
results.answer:
**Not clearly. The tool's fixed rule says "improving", but the decline is slight and the end of the period is worse than the start.**

The tool counted problem bursts per week, meaning recurrences of patterns judged to be real faults. There were 1,198 bursts from 2005-09-01 to 2005-11-29.

- **Slope:** -1.332 bursts per week, per week.
- **Half means:** 87.43 bursts per week in the first half, 83.71 in the second. That is about a 4% drop.
- **Rule:** slope below 0 and a lower second-half mean gives "improving".

**Weekly problem bursts** (week starting on the date shown):

| Week starting | Bursts |
|---|---|
| 08-29 (partial, Sep 1–4 only) | 130 |
| 09-05 | 89 |
| 09-12 | 48 |
| 09-19 | 99 |
| 09-26 | 115 |
| 10-03 | 72 |
| 10-10 | 59 |
| 10-17 | 86 |
| 10-24 | 85 |
| 10-31 | 46 |
| 11-07 | 80 |
| 11-14 | 154 |
| 11-21 | 117 |
| 11-28 (partial) | 18 |

**Why I would not call it improving:**
- **Noisy series:** weekly counts swing between 46 and 154, and the small drop in the half means sits well within that noise.
- **Partial weeks:** the first and last buckets are partial. The first one (130 bursts, Sep 1–4) pulls the slope down, and the last one (18) is nearly empty.
- **Worst weeks at the end:** the two highest full weeks are 11-14 (154) and 11-21 (117). The best stretch was early to mid-October and the week of 10-31.

**By team** (slope in bursts per week, per week):

| Team | Bursts | Slope |
|---|---|---|
| node-platform | 775 | -0.398 |
| hpc-workloads | 245 | -0.578 |
| cluster-control | 178 | -0.356 |

All three slopes are slightly negative, so no single team is driving the result. They share the same distortion from the partial first week.

**Conclusion:** the trend is flat to marginally down, with no sustained improvement. The sharp rise in mid-to-late November is worth investigating before anyone reports a reliability gain. These are counts of recurring log patterns, not confirmed incidents or impact.

results.question: Did any kinds of messages appear on BGL from 2005-12-01 to 2005-12-08 that had never been seen before? Which look like real problems?
results.answer:
Yes. 23 message patterns appeared on BGL between 2005-12-01 and 2005-12-08 that had never been seen earlier in the dataset. Of these, 12 look like real problems. That judgment comes from the stored per-pattern score (p_problem ≥ 0.5), not from my own reading of each message. Counts are log lines, and they are counted up to 2005-12-08.

**Likely real problems (12)**

Most are job or application failures: bad program images, missing directories and core dumps. Only one is a possible hardware or kernel fault.

*Application (APP) errors, hpc-workloads team*
- **Pattern 1061, first seen 12-07 08:08:** `ciod: Error loading …/sppm_chkpt/sppm: not a CNK program image`. It hit 1,024 nodes with 1,024 lines (p=0.856, "system software failure").
- **Pattern 1059, first seen 12-06 05:50:** `ciod: Error loading …/linpack…/xhpl…: invalid or missing program image, Permission denied`. It hit 1,016 nodes with 1,016 lines (p=0.846).
- **Pattern 1057, first seen 12-03 13:27:** `ciod: LOGIN chdir(/p/gb/rfisher/StirTurbDirect/…) failed: No such file or directory`. It produced 256 lines on 128 nodes (p=0.828, "network or I/O failure").
- **Pattern 1049, first seen 12-02 07:52:** `ciod: LOGIN chdir(/g/g…/loewe/romio_tests) failed: No such file or directory`. It produced 32 lines on 8 nodes.
- **Pattern 1048, first seen 12-02 07:49:** `ciod: LOGIN chdir(/home/loewe/romio_testsuite) failed: No such file or directory`. It produced 16 lines on 8 nodes.
- **Pattern 1058, first seen 12-04 11:36:** `ciod: Error loading …/rfisher/FLASH…/flash…: invalid or missing program image, No such file or directory`. It produced 8 lines on 8 nodes.

*Core dumps (KERNEL), node-platform team*
- **Pattern 1056, first seen 12-03 13:15:** core files generated for the FLASH `StirTurbDirect` program. It produced 144 lines on 72 nodes (p=0.561).
- **Pattern 1054, first seen 12-03 11:17:** core files generated for the FLASH `StirTurbPnet` program. It produced 12 lines on 10 nodes (p=0.662).
- **Pattern 1051, first seen 12-03 00:16:** core files generated for the `mem_err/merr` test program. It produced 1 line.
- **Pattern 1060, first seen 12-07 07:31:** core files generated for `HPL/xhpl`. It produced 1 line.
- **Pattern 1062, first seen 12-07 09:45:** core files generated for `auselton/bgl/mib`. It produced 1 line.

*Possible hardware or kernel fault*
- **Pattern 1053, first seen 12-03 07:57:** `instruction TLB error interrupt`. It appeared once, on one node (p=0.766, "system software failure"). It's rare, but it is the only new message that points at the machine and not at a user job.

**New but probably benign (11)**
- **Correctable-error and interrupt reporting (KERNEL):**
  - Pattern 1052, `ddr: Suppressing further CE interrupts`: 104 lines, 67 nodes, p=0.129.
  - Pattern 1050, the corrected SRAM error threshold message: 15 lines, 3 nodes, p=0.094.
  - Pattern 1063, a single torus sender retransmission message that was detected and corrected: p=0.056.
- **Counter-dump variants of the "rbs signal handler" and "total interrupts" messages:** patterns 1041–1047 differ only in how the numbers are formatted, as decimal or hex. Patterns 1041 and 1042 are huge, about 135,000 lines each across about 65,500 nodes. All score p ≤ 0.05.
- **Pattern 1055, integer alignment exceptions:** 22,177 lines on 15,258 nodes, p=0.174. It is high volume but judged not a problem.

**Caveats**
- The "new" label means the message template was first seen in this window. It does not mean a new fault.
- Many of these patterns differ only by the file or program path in the message. They are therefore best read as a few user or job issues, not 12 separate problems:
  - program images that are missing, wrong or not permitted
  - working directories that are missing
  - crashing FLASH, HPL and test runs
- The two largest events are 1,024 and 1,016 nodes failing to load a program image, on 12-07 and 12-06. They were each a single burst, which points to one bad job launch each. They do not point to 1,000 separate node faults.

results.question: Why did the OpenStack API return HTTP 503, when did it happen, and what happened around those requests?
results.answer:
**Why:** The 503s came from a failed token check, not from nova-api itself. For each failing request, nova-api called the identity service to validate the auth token. The identity side returned a 503 with an HTML error page, so nova-api could not validate the token and returned 503 to the client. The logs don't say why the identity service returned 503. Nothing from it is in this dataset.

**When:** There are only two 503 responses in the whole OpenStack dataset, both from `nova-api`:

| Time | Request | Client call |
|---|---|---|
| 2017-05-16 06:25:02.870 | `req-1cc7d50c-25a2-46b0-a668-9c00f589160c` | `GET /v2/54fadb412c4e40cdbaed9335e4c35a9e/servers/detail`, 8.1 ms |
| 2017-05-17 06:25:03.049 | `req-abcdb287-429c-40a5-8e79-d490d4fb7410` | the same call, 10.2 ms |

The two events happened almost exactly 24 hours apart. That could point to something scheduled, but I did not run a periodicity check, so treat it as a hypothesis.

**What happened around them:** Both requests logged the same four lines within about 3 ms:
1. **`ERROR`:** "Bad response code while validating token: 503".
2. **`WARNING`:** "Identity response: <!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//IETF//DTD HTML 2.0//EN">". This is the start of an HTML error page, which suggests a web server or proxy answered instead of the identity API. That is an inference from the snippet.
3. **`CRITICAL`:** "Unable to validate token: Failed to fetch token data from identity server".
4. **`INFO`:** the access-log line with `status: 503 len: 323`.

- **Before:** Each failing request's previous call had succeeded. In the first case the same request id returned 200 with a 278 ms latency one second earlier, and in the second case the same request id returned 200 with a 262 ms latency.
- **Surrounding traffic:** In the minute before each failure, the identical `servers/detail` calls were all returning 200 in about 250–450 ms.
- **After:** Normal traffic resumed within seconds. On 05-17, `nova-compute` finished a VM spawn (21.39 s) and `nova-api` served 200s for metadata and server-list calls.
- **Scope:** The failure was transient and isolated to these two requests. I found no other errors or 5xx responses in these windows. The `nova-compute` lines (periodic image checks, resource audits, one VM spawning) look unrelated.

To find the root cause, check the identity service (Keystone) and any proxy in front of it around 06:25 on both days. This dataset has no logs from them.

results.question: Do the failed password attempts on the SSH server follow a daily rhythm? At what hour are they worst?
results.answer:
**No, the failed password attempts don't follow a daily rhythm.** They are spread across all 24 hours, and no hour stands out as the worst.

I counted bursts (recurrences of a message, split by more than 30 minutes of quiet) by hour of day. I did not count raw lines per hour.

- **Main pattern, "Failed password for <*> from <IP>"** (258 bursts, 140,768 lines): bursts run at about 7–18 per hour in every hour. The highest is 08:00 with 18 bursts, about 7% of the total. Next are 23:00 with 16, and 12:00 and 16:00 with 14 each. The lowest hours are 15:00 and 11:00 with 7 each. That is too flat to call a peak, and the tool's "time-of-day pattern" rule needs one hour to hold at least 30% of bursts.
- **"Failed password for invalid user" pattern** (171 bursts, 19,848 lines): also flat, at 4–11 bursts per hour. Its highest hour is 23:00 with 11, then 19:00 and 20:00 with 10 each. That is a different peak hour from the main pattern, which again points to no daily cycle.
- **No schedule:** the gaps between bursts are irregular. Only 27.6% of gaps fall within ±20% of the median for the main pattern, and 24.1% for the invalid-user pattern. The tool's reading is "no regular schedule" for both.
- **Weekday:** there is a weak lean towards the weekend. For the main pattern, Saturday has 50 bursts and Sunday 41, against 25–36 on Tuesday to Thursday. Friday has 43 and Monday 36. For the invalid-user pattern, Saturday and Sunday have 34 each. This is a hint, not a rhythm.

Volume is driven by multi-day campaigns, not by time of day. Daily "failed password" lines swing widely over the 28 days:
- They peak at 31,843 lines on 2018-01-03, with 24,732 on 01-02 and 27,342 on 01-04.
- There are other surges of 12,000–14,000 lines a day on Dec 10, Dec 12, Dec 17, Dec 30 and Jan 1.
- They fall to quiet days of about 600–1,600 lines.
- There are no lines at all from Dec 24 to Dec 28.

If you want to rate the risk, look at which days and which source IPs are active, not which hour. I can pull the top attacker IPs for the Jan 2–4 surge if that helps.

| IP | Lines | Active |
|---|---|---|
| 59.63.188.30 | 57,539 | 2018-01-03 to 01-05 |
| 183.63.110.206 | 52,020 | 2018-01-02 to 01-03 |

**3. Successful logins, to verify**

- **61.187.54.9** has 12 accepted logins. Its first contact, on 2018-01-02 at 16:14, was a failed attempt for user `curi`, followed by an accepted login a few seconds later. It then logged in repeatedly until 2018-01-03 14:20. The same account, `curi`, normally logs in from 137.189.x.x and 14.17.22.31.

results.question: Which problems recurred most in the ZooKeeper ensemble between 2015-07-29 and 2015-08-26, which teams own them, and what should be investigated first?
results.answer:
**ZooKeeper problems, 2015-07-29 to 2015-08-26**

Two teams own all 11 problem patterns in this window. The ranking uses the burst-based priority score. A burst is a recurrence of a pattern after more than 30 minutes of quiet.

**coordination-platform: 35 bursts across 7 patterns, 13,585 lines**
- **"Cannot open channel to N at election address /IP"** (QuorumCnxManager, WARN) is the top coordination-platform item, scoring 86.4. It has 8 bursts, 2,584 lines, and is active in all 5 weeks.
  - Its largest burst ran from 2015-08-24 15:26:57 to 2015-08-25 11:23:57, with 2,417 lines.
  - That burst began right after the 4 ensemble servers started up and entered leader election (LOOKING).
  - It was accompanied by 1,203 "Notification time out" lines.
  - Peer 2 at 10.10.34.12:3888 was among those that could not be reached.
  - Following began around 11:14 on 08-25.
- **"Unexpected exception causing shutdown while sock still open"** (LearnerHandler, ERROR) has 7 bursts and 590 lines. It has the highest fault probability of any pattern here (p_fault 0.95).
- **"Exception when following the leader"** (Follower) has 6 bursts.
- **"Connection broken for id N…"** (RecvWorker) has 6 bursts. A separate variant of the same message, with a hex id, produced a single burst of 10,356 lines on 07-29. That burst is the largest line volume in the period.
- **"Unexpected exception, tries=N, connecting to /IP"** (Learner) has 5 bursts.
- **"Exception when using channel… Broken pipe"** (SendWorker) has 2 bursts.

**client-connectivity: 30 bursts across 4 patterns, 1,864 lines**
- **"caught end of stream exception"** (NIOServerCnxn, WARN) is the most frequent pattern overall, with 18 bursts and 1,670 lines. It ranks first, scoring 89.5. It was active in 3 weeks. Its fault probability (p_fault 0.58) is the lowest of the top patterns.
- **"Unexpected Exception:"** (NIOServerCnxn, ERROR) has 9 bursts but only 27 lines.
- **"Exception causing close of session… ZooKeeperServer not running"** has 2 bursts and 159 lines.
- **"…Connection reset by peer"** has 1 burst and 8 lines.

**Timing:** Warning volume was heavily front-loaded. Of 48,507 WARN lines in the window, 42,668 fell on 07-29, followed by 1,589 on 07-30 and 840 on 07-31. After that it was quiet, apart from smaller flare-ups on 08-10, 08-20, 08-24 and 08-25.

**What to investigate first**
1. **Quorum and election connectivity (coordination-platform).**
   - Start with the "Cannot open channel" pattern and the 08-24 to 08-25 episode. Check why the election port 3888 on peer 2 (10.10.34.12) was unreachable after the restart. Possible causes are a peer that was down or slow to start, a network or firewall problem, or a wrong address in the config.
   - Then look at the 07-29 storm, which started around 19:03 to 19:04: the "Connection broken", LearnerHandler shutdown and "ZooKeeperServer not running" lines. These point to a leader or follower failure and re-election.
   - Compare the 07-29 storm with the 08-24 episode to see whether they share a cause.
2. **Client-connectivity.** Look at the "end of stream" and "Unexpected Exception" lines only afterwards. They are the most frequent, but they are probably client disconnects that follow the server instability.

**Caveats**
- ZooKeeper logs carry no node or host field, so I can't say whether this is one bad server or the whole ensemble.

results.question: In ZooKeeper, what else tends to happen at the same time as "caught end of stream exception"?
results.answer:
In ZooKeeper, "caught end of stream exception" (pattern 200062, NIOServerCnxn) is part of a client-session teardown and reconnect sequence. I measured this over its 18 bursts, counting other patterns that start within ±300 s. The control is the same bursts shifted one day earlier.

**Almost always present (18 of 18 bursts, lift ≈ 17.9 against a control share of 0.056):**
- "Closed socket connection for client /<IP> which had sessionid <HEX>". This also appears on the same node in all 18 cases.
- "Processed session termination for sessionid: <HEX>"
- "Expiring session <HEX>, timeout of <N>ms exceeded"

**Often present (13 of 18 bursts, 72%, lift ≈ 12.9):**
- "Accepted socket connection from /<IP>"
- "Connection request from old client /<IP>; will be dropped if server is in r-o mode"
- "Client attempting to establish new session at /<IP>"
- "Established session <HEX> with negotiated timeout <N> for client /<IP>"

These four lines are a client reconnecting and getting a new session.

**Occasional (lower lift, small counts):**
- "Got zxid <HEX> expected <N>x1": 5 of 18 bursts.
- "Creating new log file: log.<HEX>": 4 of 18 bursts.
- "Unexpected Exception:": 2 of 18 bursts.
- Single cases of "LOOKING" and "Notification time out".
- Single same-node cases of "Exception causing close of session … ZooKeeperServer not running" and "Closed socket connection … (no session established for client)".

**Reading:** the usual picture is that a client connection drops. The server logs the end-of-stream exception, closes the socket, and expires and terminates the session. In most cases the client then reconnects and gets a new session.

This is an association in time, not proof of cause. The leader-election lines (LOOKING, notification time-out) appear in only one burst, so they are not a typical companion.

results.question: Based on the Apache web server error log from 2005-12-01 to 2006-03-01, what should we prioritise next?
results.answer:
**Priority 1: "script not found or unable to stat" (web-platform, httpd).** It is the top-ranked problem pattern, with a score of 89.5.

- **Two variants.** Pattern 300042 is the bare message: 3,339 lines and 127 bursts, up from 29 in the previous period. Pattern 300033 is the `[client <IP>] … <PATH>` form: 2,207 lines and 77 bursts, up from 32. Together they are the largest and fastest-growing problem in the period.
- **What it hits.** In 300033, almost all the lines name two paths. `/var/www/cgi-bin/awstats.pl` has 1,101 lines and `/var/www/cgi-bin/awstats` has 1,083.
- **Timing.** The search term "script not found" has 0 lines in the weeks of 5 Dec to 26 Dec. It returns from the week of 2 Jan, at 259–1,017 lines per week through February. It is steady, not a one-off burst.
- **Source.** 86 client IPs are involved. The biggest, 211.99.203.228, has only 80 lines, so no single client dominates.
- **Likely cause.** This looks like scanning or probing for awstats, or a missing or misconfigured awstats CGI. That is my hypothesis, not something the logs prove.
- **Action.** Either install or fix awstats, or block and ignore those requests.

**Priority 2: mod_jk / jk2 (app-integration).**
- `jk2_init() Can't find child <N> in scoreboard` (300022) ranks second with a score of 87.5. It has 415 lines and 69 bursts (up from 54), and it was active in 13 of the 14 weeks.
- `mod_jk child workerEnv in error state` (300040) has 1,623 lines. Its bursts fell from 160 to 71, so it is improving, but it is still high in volume.
- `script not found or unable to stat` under mod_jk (300046) has 263 lines and 24 bursts, up from 17.
- All three are Apache–Tomcat connector faults, so look at the worker and scoreboard configuration together.

**Lower priority:**
- **Startup errors.** The `worker.jni` / `channel.jni` / `vm` errors (`config.update()` and `env.createBean2()`) have 11 lines each and are falling (11 bursts, from 16). Ranks 4–10 are all these startup errors. They fire together, so one jk2 configuration fix should clear them.
- **Directory index forbidden.** Pattern 300020 has 1,650 lines but its bursts are falling (853, from 1,045). Its stored judgment is "not a problem" (p_fault 0.12), so don't spend time on it.

**Team view.** web-platform has 17 problem patterns and 1,205 bursts, down from 1,331. app-integration has 3 patterns and 164 bursts, down from 231. Overall volume is falling, but the "script not found" patterns are growing against that trend.

**Limits.**
- Apache logs no host, so I can't say how widely a problem is spread.
- Cost, downtime and customer impact are not in these logs.

results.question: What happened to HDFS block blk_-1608999687919862906, step by step?
results.answer:
Block `blk_-1608999687919862906` was written, replicated to 10 datanodes, read many times, and then deleted. The logs show no errors or warnings for it. All 269 lines are INFO, from 2008-11-09 20:35:18 to 21:38:40. The block is the `job.jar` for MapReduce job `job_200811092030_0001`.

**1. Allocation and first write (20:35:18–20:35:19)**
- The NameNode (`dfs.FSNamesystem`) allocated the block for `/mnt/hadoop/mapred/system/job_200811092030_0001/job.jar`.
- Three datanodes started receiving it: 10.250.19.102, 10.250.10.6 and 10.250.14.224.
- The `PacketResponder` threads (0, 1 and 2) terminated.
- Each datanode logged "Received block … of size 91178".
- The NameNode logged `addStoredBlock` for 10.250.10.6, 10.251.111.209 and 10.250.14.224.

**2. Replication to more nodes (20:35:21–20:35:32)**
- The NameNode asked 10.250.14.224 to replicate the block to 10.251.215.16 and 10.251.71.193. That node started a transfer thread and logged "Transmitted block".
- Chained requests followed:
  - 10.251.215.16 was asked to copy to 10.251.74.79 and 10.251.107.19 (20:35:24–26).
  - 10.251.107.19 was asked to copy to 10.251.31.5 and 10.251.71.240 (20:35:27–28).
  - 10.251.31.5 was asked to copy to 10.251.90.64 (20:35:30–31).
- The block was added to the block map on each new node. The last one was 10.251.90.64 at 20:35:32.
- That makes 10 replica holders in all. Every copy was 91178 bytes.

**3. Heavy read traffic (20:35:23–20:36:26)**
- There are 203 "Served block … to /<client>" lines. They come from the datanodes holding replicas, such as 10.250.10.6, 10.250.14.224, 10.251.111.209, 10.251.215.16, 10.251.74.79 and 10.251.107.19.
- This is consistent with many task nodes fetching the job jar at job start. The first lines are at 20:35:23 and the last at 20:36:26.

**4. Quiet period**
- About 1 hour 2 minutes passes with no activity for this block.

**5. Deletion (21:38:09–21:38:40)**
- At 21:38:09 the NameSystem logged `NameSystem.delete` and added the block to the `invalidSet` of all 10 replica nodes. Those are the 10 nodes that had stored it.
- From 21:38:10 to 21:38:40, `dfs.FSDataset` logged 10 "Deleting block … file /mnt/hadoop/dfs/data/current/blk_-1608999687919862906" lines. The last was at 21:38:40.
- This matches normal cleanup after the job finished. The logs don't state that cause, so I'm inferring it.

results.question: Which HDFS errors or warnings are the most frequent, and are they limited to a few datanodes?
results.answer:
HDFS has no ERROR lines. It has only INFO and WARN, and the WARN lines (362,793 in total) are not limited to a few datanodes.

**Most frequent warnings**

| Pattern | Lines | Share of WARN |
|---|---|---|
| `Got exception while serving blk_… to /<IP>` (dfs.DataNode$DataXceiver, datanode-ops) | 356,207 | 98.2% |
| `Unexpected error trying to delete block … BlockInfo not found in volumeMap` (dfs.FSDataset, storage-platform) | 5,545 | 1.5% |
| `addStoredBlock: Redundant addStoredBlock request received` (dfs.FSNamesystem, namenode-platform) | 975 | 0.3% |
| `PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block …` | 47 | <0.1% |
| `Adding an already existing block …` (dfs.DataBlockScanner) | 10 | <0.1% |
| `Failed to transfer blk_… to <IP> … Connection reset by peer` (dfs.DataNode$DataTransfer) | 9 | <0.1% |

- **Serving exception:** the stored judgment (p_fault 0.76) labels it a network or I/O failure. The first one was logged on 2008-11-09 at 21:38:49, and it came in 8 bursts.
- **Delete-block warning:** also judged a network or I/O failure (p_fault 0.78). It came in 18 bursts.

**Spread across datanodes**

HDFS lines carry no node or host field, so I couldn't use the node-spread tool. I used the IP addresses inside the messages instead. The serving-exception warning mentions 202 distinct IPs in 670,527 mentions. The mentions include both datanode and client addresses, so 202 is not a datanode count.

The top IPs each appear in about 3,460–3,610 lines, and the counts fall off only slowly. They are all active over the same period, from 2008-11-09 21:38 to 2008-11-11 about 02:30. The warning is therefore cluster-wide, not tied to a few datanodes. The IP counts show no sign of a hot node.

I couldn't check the spread of the delete-block warning, because its messages contain no IPs.

results.question: In HDFS, what happens right before "PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block" events, and how often do they occur?
results.answer:
In HDFS, the "PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block" warning appears 47 times, in 7 bursts. It follows a wave of DataNode write-pipeline errors that starts roughly 12–13 minutes earlier. The link is an association in time, not a proven cause.

**How often**
- The pattern is 500054, a WARN from `dfs.PendingReplicationBlocks$PendingReplicationMonitor`, owned by storage-platform.
- All 47 lines fall between 2008-11-10 10:49:36 and 2008-11-11 09:24:33, a span of about 22.6 hours.
- Lines come in same-second batches of several blocks. For example, 5 lines at 21:24:35 and 4 or more at 22:29:35.
- Hourly line counts:
  - 2008-11-10: 10:00 had 1, 21:00 had 5, 22:00 had 8.
  - 2008-11-11: 05:00 had 6, 07:00 had 16, 08:00 had 8, 09:00 had 3.
  - Every other hour had none.
- The biggest burst (16 lines) ran 07:14:34–07:29:33 on 2008-11-11.

**What comes right before**

I checked the 7 bursts against a 15-minute look-back. In the largest burst, the preceding activity started about 15 minutes earlier:
- **06:59:43:** a WARN, "NameSystem.addStoredBlock: Redundant addStoredBlock request received" (pattern 500024), the first problem-level line.
- **07:00:19 onward:** `writeBlock … Could not read from stream` errors.
- **07:00:59 onward:** a cluster of write-pipeline errors:
  - `Connection reset by peer`
  - `EOFException`
  - `InterruptedIOException`
  - `PacketResponder … Interrupted`
  - `ClosedByInterruptException`
  - "Changing block file offset" lines
- The timeouts then start at 07:14:34. That is about 13–14 minutes after the errors begin, consistent with the median lead times of 540–802 s (about 9–13 minutes).

Across all 7 bursts, the most common precursors each preceded only 2–3 of the 7 bursts, so they are suggestive, not consistent:
- "Changing block file offset of block…" (pattern 500027) preceded 3 bursts, median lead 754 s.
- `ClosedByInterruptException` (pattern 500051) preceded 3 bursts, median lead 760 s.
- `Connection reset by peer`, `EOFException`, `SocketTimeoutException`, "Received block" and "Receiving empty packet" each preceded 2 bursts, with median leads of 540–802 s.
- The same precursors did not appear in the same look-back window one day earlier, which is what the lift of 2–3 reflects.

**Reading (hypothesis)**

Network or I/O failures during block writes seem to leave blocks under-replicated. Their replication requests then expire in the pending-replication queue and the monitor logs a timeout. The stored judgment for this pattern also says "network or I/O", with p_problem 0.665.

results.question: Why are orders failing in the demo shop, and which service is the source?
results.answer:
**Short answer:** Most failed orders trace back to the **payment** service, which logs "Visa cache full: cannot add new item." A smaller second failure comes from the **currency** service being unreachable. The frontend only reports these errors; it isn't where they start.

This covers the OTel demo slice, 2025-09-23 00:00–00:29. The slice holds 0.1 s of every minute, so line counts are for the sample, not the full traffic.

**1. Payment: "Visa cache full" (largest cause)**
- The frontend logs "Failed to place order" 21,821 times (pattern 600005). The same wording appears inside the other frontend error patterns, so this count overlaps with them.
- The biggest error pattern, 26,122 lines, reads `failed to charge card: could not charge the card: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = Visa cache full: cannot add new item.` The same text appears in several other frontend error patterns.
- The payment service logs the original error as "Visa cache full: cannot add new item." (pattern 600010, 11,253 lines on 24 nodes). It logs 23,984 ERROR lines in total, across those 24 nodes.
- It starts at 00:00:00 and runs through the whole window, so it is a persistent fault rather than a blip.
- I could not follow a single request from payment through the frontend. The sampled trace ID I checked only contains the payment line.

**2. Currency conversion (second failure path)**
- The frontend also logs `failed to convert shipping cost to currency … code = Unavailable`. The detail is either `connection refused` or `connection reset by peer` / `EOF`.
- There are further errors reading `failed to prepare order: failed to convert price of "<ID>" to USD`. For example, pattern 600040 has 6,190 lines and 600044 has 6,184. Both go through the same currency conversion.
- That points to the **currency** service being unreachable or restarting. I did not find a direct crash message from it.
- The currency service itself logs only 199 ERROR lines. They are OpenTelemetry exporter failures, `data refused due to high memory usage`, which suggests memory pressure on the telemetry collector. That is a hypothesis; the logs don't show it causing the order failures.

**Minor and not the cause:** checkout logs "failed to send order confirmation … email service: expected 200, got 500". It is a warning-level message that checkout logs at ERROR, and it comes after the order step.

**Source:** payment ("Visa cache full") is the primary source, owned by payments-team. The currency service is a secondary source. The frontend is only where the errors show up.

results.question: Follow trace 68a1dd0d5118a650745a1e0fcd04105f in the demo shop through the services. Where did it go wrong?
results.answer:
**The trace failed in the payment service, and the error then came back up to the frontend.** Four log lines carry this trace ID. They span about 52 ms, from 00:19:00.014 to 00:19:00.066 on 2025-09-23. All four were logged on one node, `gke-clickstack-demo-2-default-pool-a93db85f-67cb`.

| Time | Service | Severity | What it logged |
|---|---|---|---|
| 00:19:00.014822 | frontend | TRACE | "Checkout" (the order starts, with an empty `currencyCode`). |
| 00:19:00.054380 | payment | INFO | "Charge request received." The request is for USD, units low 1016 and nanos 449999990, paid with a Visa card. |
| 00:19:00.064622 | payment | ERROR | An error line with only the span and trace IDs and no message text. |
| 00:19:00.066664 | frontend | ERROR | "Failed to place order", gRPC error code 13. The details read: "failed to charge card: could not charge the card: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = Visa cache full: cannot add new item." |

**Where it went wrong:** the charge step in the payment service. About 10 ms after it received the charge request, it logged an error. The frontend's error message gives the cause as "Visa cache full: cannot add new item." The frontend's "Failed to place order" line comes about 2 ms after the payment error. That fits the payment failure being passed straight back to the user's checkout. It is my reading of the timing, not something the logs state outright.

**Limits of this trace:**
- No other service (cart, checkout, shipping or email) logged under this trace ID. I can't say whether other services were involved or whether the failure stopped the flow early.
- The payment ERROR line has no text of its own. The cause comes only from the frontend's error details.
